## Exercise 1

According to the model, a one-unit increase in PRS is associated with a 0.03 decrease in the predicted FEV1/FVC ratio for individuals with 10 or fewer pack-years of smoking, holding all the other variables constant. As a result, this relationship becomes more negative as pack-years increase.

## Exercise 2

Yes, there is statistically significant evidence that the relationship between PRS and FEV1/FVC depends on pack-years of smoking. All interaction terms have p-values less than 0.001, indicating that the relationship differs depending on smoking history.

## Exercise 3

Holding all the other variables constant, individuals with more than 50 pack-years of smoking are predicted to have an FEV1/FVC ratio 0.04 lower than individuals with 10 or fewer pack-years when PRS is zero.

## Exercise 4

According to the model, a one-unit increase in fruit availability is associated with a 0.028 decrease in predicted daily travel distance when frugivory is zero, holding all the other variables constant. The interaction coefficient of −0.130 indicates that the relationship becomes more negative as frugivory increases.

## Exercise 5

Holding all the other variables constant, a one-unit increase in frugivory is associated with a 0.041 decrease in predicted daily travel distance when fruit availability is zero. Since frugivory is a proportion, this represents an increase from 0 to 1.

## Exercise 6

Yes, the figure suggests that the effect of Prop 56 on smoking prevalence depends on income status. For low-income adults, predicted smoking prevalence decreased from 14.0% to 6.8%, a decrease of 7.2 percentage points. However, for high-income adults, it only decreased from 4.5% to 4.2%, a decrease of 0.3 percentage points. The confidence intervals do not overlap for low-income adults, while they overlap for high-income adults. This suggests that the effect was greater for low-income adults, although a formal interaction test would be needed to confirm the statistical significance.
